title: Do you have to wear hijab in front of your mother's uncle?
headline: A mother's uncle is a mahram; the majority of jurists and recent fatwas agree

summary.text: The majority of jurists hold that a mother's uncle, whether paternal or maternal, is one of a woman's mahrams, so she need not wear hijab before him. Al-Sha'bi and ʿIkrima held that uncles are not mahrams, and ʿIkrima explained the omission in Quran 24:31 by saying the two are named through their sons. Recent fatwas state plainly that she may take off her hijab before them, shake hands and be alone with them.

Ruling on a woman uncovering herself before her husband's brother, her uncle, and her maternal uncle

paragraphs.text: The verse that sets out who a woman may appear before without full covering is Quran 24:31, and it does not name uncles; the list runs through husbands, fathers, husbands' fathers, sons, husbands' sons, brothers, brothers' sons, sisters' sons, their women, slaves, male attendants without desire and small children. The verse that fixes the permanently forbidden degrees is Quran 4:23, which prohibits mothers, daughters, sisters, father's sisters, mother's sisters, brothers' daughters and sisters' daughters. The jurists reasoned from the aunts named there to the corresponding men: if a man's maternal aunt is permanently forbidden to him, her brother, your mother's uncle, stands in the same degree of kinship to you. Quran 33:55 gives a shorter list for the Prophet's wives, and the footnote to it states that the brothers of both parents, the uncles, are included as "fathers" or "parents" according to hadith.

"Indeed, a man's paternal uncle is the like of his father" is recorded in Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3760; Tirmidhi called it hasan sahih, and Ahmad Muhammad Shakir, al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai all graded it sahih. The same meaning comes from Abu Hurayra: "Al-Abbas is the uncle of the Messenger of Allah, and indeed a man's uncle is like his father's brother," which Tirmidhi called hasan gharib and the same three graders marked sahih. A route of it in Musnad Ahmad was graded da'if by Darussalam, as Ibn Uthaymeen notes.

"What is forbidden by blood ties is forbidden by breastfeeding" (Sunan an-Nasa'i 3302) is graded sahih by Abu Ghuddah and al-Albani and agreed upon by Zubair Ali Zai, and the Prophet ﷺ applied it when he declined to marry Hamza's daughter, saying she was his brother's daughter through nursing. This matters because foster-mahrams are also absent from 24:31 yet are certainly mahrams, which shows the verse is not an exhaustive list. The hadith forbidding marriage to a woman and her paternal or maternal aunt at once is sahih in Muslim, and Ibn Shihab added that a woman's father's aunt and mother's aunt are in the same position.

In the Hanafi school, al-Hidaya, in the chapter on intercourse, looking and touching, defines a mahram as one permanently unlawful by lineage, fosterage or marriage; looking at what may be seen of mahrams is permitted, and touching what may be looked at is permitted when desire is not feared. Darul Iftaa Chicago, quoting al-Hidaya, classes the head and chest among the "inner adornment" mahrams may see, while an IslamOnline summary gives the Hanafi and Shafi'i limit as navel to knee.

In the Shafi'i school, Rawdat al-Talibin holds that the mahram does not look at what is between the navel and the knee and may look at the rest according to the madhhab. Mughni al-Muhtaj adds that what shows during work may be seen, the navel-to-knee area is forbidden, and the dispute concerns what lies between; there is no difference between a Muslim and a non-Muslim mahram unless the latter considers maharim lawful, like the Magians. The navel-to-knee area is the "minor" awrah, to be covered even from women.

In the Maliki school, Hashiyat al-Dasuqi on al-Dardir, with al-Sawi's gloss, states that it is forbidden for the mahram to see her chest, and the Shafi'i allowance of everything but the navel-to-knee area is described as a leniency (fusḥa). Before a non-mahram Muslim man her awrah is everything but the face and palms.

In the Hanbali school, al-Mughni holds that he may look at what usually shows, such as the neck, head, palms and feet, and may not look at what is usually covered, such as the chest and back; Ahmad answered the question with 24:31. Kashshaf al-Qina' lists the face, neck, hand, foot, head and shin, and defines the mahram as one permanently forbidden by lineage or a permissible cause. Read together, all four allow the head and hair to be uncovered before a mahram, and they differ over the chest, the back and the area between navel and knee. The command to lower the gaze in 24:30 still stands for the man in front of whom she sits, mahram or not.

Scholars gave several reasons for the silence of 24:31, gathered in a recent fatwa: the list follows the people who most often enter a woman's house, and uncles usually do not live with her, so covering before them is not burdensome; they are included under the word "fathers," since the Prophet ﷺ said a man's uncle is like his father; if a brother's son and a sister's son may see her, her uncle is even more obviously permitted; and the verse was not meant to exhaust every mahram, just as it does not mention foster-relations, which are established by hadith. Ibn Ashur in al-Tahrir wa'l-Tanwir concluded that the silence about uncles is not because their ruling differs from other mahrams, but because the verse kept to those who habitually frequent the house. As a Companion practice, Ibn al-Arabi reports in Ahkam al-Quran, as quoted by IslamOnline, that Safiyya bint Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's ﷺ aunt, did not cover her head before him or before ten of the first Muhajirun, meaning her sons and her sisters' sons.

The aunt hadith is about combining two women in one marriage, not about mahramiyya, which is why a man is not a mahram to his wife's aunt and may marry her after his wife dies or is divorced. The Shafi'i breadth is explained as a leniency for need, such as a mother nursing her child in front of a mahram in a small space. Ibn Baz treats the face as awrah before non-mahram men but not before mahrams like the father, brother or paternal uncle; the hadith of Asma on face and hands was called mursal by Abu Dawud himself, graded sahih by al-Albani and Muhammad Muhyi al-Din and da'if by Zubair Ali Zai, and al-Albani strengthened it with the Asma bint Umays route in al-Bayhaqi. The uncle's mahram status is unaffected by doubts about his birth, since the majority hold a maternal uncle is a mahram even if he was born of zina.

The Permanent Committee, quoted by IslamQA, was asked exactly this question about the mother's paternal and maternal uncles and answered that she may take off her hijab before them, shake hands and be alone with them, since the mother's uncle and the father's uncle stand in the position of brothers' and sisters' sons in kinship, so the ruling on showing adornment is the same for all of them. Ibn Uthaymeen, in al-Fatawa al-Jami'a li'l-Mar'ah al-Muslimah, answered that a mother's or father's paternal or maternal uncle is a mahram, because your father's paternal uncle is your paternal uncle and your father's maternal uncle is your maternal uncle. Ibn Baz said the same: your mother's maternal uncle is your maternal uncle, and her mother's paternal uncle and her father's paternal uncle are your paternal uncles. Darul Iftaa Chicago gives the Hanafi application: the ascendent mahram relatives of one's parents are mahrams and all the related rulings apply to them.

On how much to uncover, Ibn Baz held that there is no harm in a mahram seeing the hair, while covering is better and more cautious, especially in this age of weak restraint. IslamOnline puts the standard at customary work clothes, with more covering being better, and adds that if desire is feared what was permitted becomes prohibited. The uncle himself is a mahram, but his son is not, so the son of your mother's uncle is a stranger to you and may marry you; likewise the daughter of your mother's paternal uncle is not a mahram, and cousin's sons generally are not mahrams. A wife's aunt is not a mahram to her husband, and a sister's husband or a husband's brother is not a mahram.
